getting-started.title: Getting Started
getting-started.description:
# Forking the Challenge Repository

Before you can complete the remaining challenges, you need your own copy of the challenge repository. This allows you to commit your work and push your solutions to GitHub.

## 1. Fork the repository

Click the **fork** button on the [challenge repository](https://github.com/{orgName}/{repoName}):

![Fork button](/github-fork-button.png)

Keep the repository name unchanged: **{repoName}**, and uncheck the "Copy the main branch only" option.

![Fork options](/github-fork-options.png)

After forking, you should see the repository under your GitHub account:

![Forked repository under your account](/github-fork-success.png)

## 2. Clone your fork locally

Click the **Code** button and copy the HTTPS URL:

![GitHub clone URL dropdown](/github-url-dropdown.png)

Inside your terminal, navigate to the folder you want to clone the challenges into. Replace *<folder>* with the absolute or relative path of your desired folder:

```sh
cd <folder>
```

Clone your fork into the folder by replacing *<url>* with the link you copied:

```sh
git clone <url>
```

Once your fork is set up, you'll be ready to continue with the rest of the challenges.

where-am-i.title: Where am I?
where-am-i.description:
Open your terminal and navigate into your cloned repo.

Somewhere in the `where-am-i/` folder there's a file containing a flag. Use the terminal to find it and read its contents. Once you find the flag, enter it below.

The following commands may be useful:

**macOS + Linux**

- `cd [directory]` - short for **change directory**, moves you into another directory.
  - `cd where-am-i` moves into the `where-am-i/` directory.
  - `cd ..` moves up to the parent directory.
  - Running `cd` without an argument returns you to your home directory.

- `ls [directory]` - short for **list**, lists files and directories inside a directory.
  - `ls` with no arguments lists the contents of the current directory.
  - `ls <directory>` lists the contents of the specified directory.

- `cat <file>` - short for **concatenate**, combines the contents of files and prints them to the terminal. When used with a single file, it simply prints that file's contents.
  - `cat <file>` requires a file as an argument.
  - You can provide multiple files, such as `cat file1.txt file2.txt`, to print them one after another.

**Windows**

- `cd [directory]` - short for **change directory**, moves you into another directory.
  - `cd where-am-i` moves into the `where-am-i/` directory.
  - `cd ..` moves up to the parent directory.
  - Running `cd` without an argument displays your current directory.

- `dir [directory]` - short for **directory**, lists files and directories in the current directory
  - `dir` with no argument lists the contents of the current directory.
  - `dir <directory>` lists the contents of the specified directory.

- `type <file>` - prints the contents of a file to the terminal
  - `type <file>` requires a file as an argument.

hidden-in-plain-sight.title: Hidden in plain sight
hidden-in-plain-sight.description:
Navigate into the `hidden-in-plain-sight/` folder.

There are many files in this folder, and one of them has the flag hidden in its filename.

List the files and look carefully.

going-deeper.title: Going deeper
going-deeper.description:
The `going-deeper/` folder contains several nested directories.

The flag is hidden inside a file somewhere at the bottom of the tree. Navigate your way down, one level at a time. Each level contains a clue telling you whether to keep going.

List the contents of each directory and follow the clues until you find the flag.

the-invisible-ones.title: The invisible ones
the-invisible-ones.description:
Navigate into the `the-invisible-ones/` folder and list its contents.

You'll see a couple of files, but the flag isn't in any of them. There's another file in the folder that doesn't appear in the default directory listing.

Some files are **hidden files**. On macOS and Linux, hidden files have a name that starts with a `.` (dot), such as `.hidden-file`. They are still part of the directory, but are normally left out of standard directory listings. They are often used for configuration files or other files that users don't need to see during normal use.

On macOS and Linux, add the `-a` flag to `ls` to show hidden files. On Windows, use the `/a` option with `dir`.

For example:

- `ls -a` - lists all files, including hidden files.
- `dir /a` - lists all files, including hidden files.

Find the hidden file and read its contents to get the flag.

first-commit.title: Your first commit
first-commit.description:
Now that you know your way around the terminal, it's time to start using Git.

Git tracks changes to files over time. A **commit** is a saved snapshot of your project at a specific point in time, like a checkpoint you can always go back to.

Inside the `first-commit/` folder, create a file called `notes.txt` and write anything you like in it.

You can use `echo` to write text directly into a file:

- `echo "<text>" > <file>` - prints `<text>` and redirects the output into the specified file.
  - For example, `echo "Hello, Git!" > notes.txt` creates `notes.txt` containing `Hello, Git!`.
  - If the file already exists, `>` **overwrites** its contents.
  - Use `>>` instead of `>` to **append** text to the end of an existing file.

After creating the file, stage, commit, and push your changes to GitHub.
Then stage, commit, and push your changes to GitHub.

A commit needs a message describing what changed. We'll use the **Conventional Commits** style:

- `feat: add notes` - `feat` is used when adding a new feature.
- `docs: add readme` - `docs` is used for documentation changes.

For this challenge, use the format `type: description`, where `type` and `description` are placeholders. Replace them with an appropriate type and a short description of your change.

You can find the full [Conventional Commits specification](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) here.

The following commands may be useful:

- `git status` - shows the current state of your repository, including which files have been changed or staged.
- `git add <file>` - **stages** a file, marking it to be included in the next commit.
  - `git add <file>` stages a specific file.
  - `git add <file1> <file2>` stages multiple specific files.
  - `git add .` stages all changes in the current directory and its subdirectories.
  - `git add -A` stages all changes in the entire repository, including changes outside the current directory.
- `git commit -m "<message>"` - creates a **commit** containing the staged changes. The `-m` option lets you provide the commit message directly.
- `git push` - uploads your local commits to the remote repository on GitHub.

edit-and-push.title: Edit and push
edit-and-push.description:
Most of your time with Git will be spent editing existing files, not creating new ones.

Open `edit-and-push/about.txt` in a text editor and fill in your name and the about section. Save the file, then stage, commit, and push your changes.

The following commands may be useful:

**macOS + Linux**

- `nano <file>` - opens a file in the **nano** terminal text editor.
  - Make your changes, then press `Ctrl+O` to save and `Ctrl+X` to exit nano.

**Windows**

- `notepad <file>` - opens a file in Windows Notepad.
  - Save the file in Notepad when you're done.

gitignore.title: Keep secrets secret
gitignore.description:
Not every file in a project should be committed. API keys, passwords, and generated files are common examples of files you don't want Git to track.

Git has a mechanism for this: a file called `.gitignore`. It contains patterns that tell Git which files and directories to ignore.

Inside `gitignore/`, create a `secrets/` folder and a file inside it called `api-key.txt`. Put anything you like in the file; pretend it contains a secret API key.

Now run:

```bash
git status
```

You should see `secrets/` listed as an untracked directory.

Your goal is to create a `.gitignore` file that tells Git to ignore the `secrets/` folder.

Once you've created it, run `git status` again and check that `secrets/` is no longer shown as untracked.

When you've confirmed that it works, stage, commit, and push your `.gitignore` file.

> **Stuck?** It's completely normal to look things up when learning Git. You can use Git's built-in help with commands such as `git help gitignore`, or search the internet for the problem you're trying to solve.

You can also read the [Git documentation](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitignore) for the `.gitignore` syntax.

find-the-bug.title: Find the bug
find-the-bug.description:
In `find-the-bug/` there's a small webpage. The page is broken, and your job is to figure out why.

Start by opening `index.html` and looking at what files the page is trying to load. You don't need to know HTML to do this: look for references to other files, such as stylesheets, images, or scripts.

You can also open the page in your browser to see what it currently looks like. From inside the `find-the-bug/` directory, you can use:

```bash
# macOS
open index.html

# Linux
xdg-open index.html

# Windows
start index.html
```

Look at the page in your browser, then compare what `index.html` expects with the files that are actually present in the repository.

The following commands may be useful:

**macOS + Linux**

- `mv <source> <destination>` — moves a file or directory from one location to another.
  - For example, `mv old/file.txt new/file.txt` moves `file.txt` into the `new/` directory.

**Windows**

- `move <source> <destination>` — moves a file or directory from one location to another.
  - For example, `move old\file.txt new\file.txt` moves `file.txt` into the `new` directory.

This is the first of three challenges involving this webpage. Fix only the problem described in this challenge; the page will still have other problems afterward.

missing-images.title: Missing images
missing-images.description:
Go to `missing-images/`. This is the same project, but a new problem.

The stylesheet is in the right place now, but the page references multiple images that can't be found.

Look at what the page tries to load and identify the image files it references. You don't need to know HTML or CSS to do this: look for references to image files, such as `.png`, `.jpg`, or `.svg`.

You can search for these references using `grep` or `findstr`. If you know which file contains the reference, you can search that file directly. You can also search recursively through the entire project, which is useful when you don't know which files to look inside.

**macOS + Linux:**

- `grep "<pattern>" <file>` - searches for text or a pattern inside a file.
  - For example, `grep "hello" index.html` finds lines containing `hello` in `index.html`.
- `grep -r "<pattern>" <directory>` - searches recursively through a directory and all of its files.
  - For example, `grep -r "hello" .` searches the entire project for lines containging `hello`.

**Windows:**

- `findstr "<pattern>" <file>` - searches for text or a pattern inside a file.
  - For example, `findstr "hello" index.html` finds lines containing `hello` in `index.html`.
  - `findstr /s "<pattern>" <directory>\*` - searches recursively through files in a directory and its subdirectories.
  - For example, `findstr /s "hello" *` searches the entire project for lines containing `hello`.

Then explore the project to find where the images are actually located.

The following command may be useful:

**macOS + Linux:**

- `mv <source> <destination>` - moves files or directories to another location.
  - You can use `*` as a wildcard to match multiple files.
  - For example, `mv <path>/* <destination>` moves all files inside the `<path>` directory into the destination directory.

**Windows:**

- `move <source> <destination>` - moves files or directories to another location.
  - You can use `*` as a wildcard to match multiple files.
  - For example, `move <path>\* <destination>` moves all files inside the `<path>` directory into the destination directory.

This is the second of three challenges involving this webpage. Fix only the problem described in this challenge; there will still be another problem afterward.

broken-link.title: Broken link
broken-link.description:
The navigation in `broken-link/index.html` contains a link to an About page, but clicking it won't take you anywhere.

The file exists, but it has the wrong name. Open `index.html` and look at what filename the link expects. Then find the corresponding file and rename it to match.

The following command may be useful:

**macOS + Linux:**

- `mv <source> <destination>` - moves or renames a file or directory.
  - To rename a file, use its current name as the source and its new name as the destination.

**Windows:**

- `ren <old-name> <new-name>` - renames a file or directory.

Once you've renamed the file, commit and push your changes.

time-traveler.title: Time Traveler
time-traveler.description:
Git doesn't just track your current files, it remembers every version of every file that has ever been committed, even ones that have since been deleted, and every message written along the way.

At some point, a file appeared inside `time-traveler/` and then disappeared again. Dig through the project's history to find out what happened to it.

The flag for the challenge isn't sitting in one place, you'll need to piece it together from two different parts of the history.

Some commands that might help:

- `git log` - shows the commit history: messages, authors, and a unique hash for each commit. Read commit messages carefully, they don't always tell the whole story, but sometimes they tell you more than intended.
- `git log --oneline -- <path>` - shows only the commits that touched a specific file or folder.
- `git show <commit-hash>` - shows exactly what was added or removed in a specific commit.
- `git show <commit-hash>:<path>` - shows the full contents of a file exactly as it was at that commit, even if the file doesn't exist anymore today.
